rv.q: Great theatre can be about many things: star quality, spectacle, the lightning-in-bottle capture of a moment, the alchemical power of song or speech on a bare stage. In this Evita, all those things come triumphantly together.
You know there’s something deeply twisted under that pretty shiny surface, but, like the audiences of Evita, you’re powerless to resist.
It knocks the breath from your body and leaves you gasping, every moment taut and vibrating with passionate intensity.
The result is a total triumph, dominated by a powerhouse, reputation-restoring performance from Zegler.
It’s a pitch-perfect mix of theatrical audacity, political satire and deft cinematography.
“She’s a diamond in their dull gray lives,” sings the Argentine president Juan Domingo Perón of his wife in “Evita,” Tim Rice and Andrew Lloyd Webber’s sung-through musical about Eva Perón.
If a successful musical is simply about the singing, dancing and spectacle, this one soars.
It feels like being inside a stadium gig, a football match and a political rally all at once: exhilarating, addictive, ultimately terrifying.
This Evita is an event with a capital E, an assertion of the unique power of theatre to become both story and spectacle.

This Evita is not without its flaws, it’s rushed, flashy, and sometimes narratively thin, but it’s also thrilling, stylish, and full of theatrical bravado. Jamie Lloyd’s vision may divide opinion, but it’s never dull.
What Jamie Lloyd has done with this story and this production is nothing short of miraculous.
